02616 Large Scale Modelling · Project 2 · Gaia N-body

Parallelizing Gaia N-Body

We simulate stars from Gaia DR3 with direct-summation gravity, every star against every other, and split the work across MPI ranks. This page goes from the data, through the simulation and its runtime, to the parallel design.

David Schabert · Pelle Hesketh · Rasmus Andersen

→ ← next / previous sectionF fullscreen3D views: drag to rotate, click and scroll to zoom
The data

590,000 Gaia stars, and the ball we simulate

The cleaned Gaia DR3 sample has 589,993 stars with a positive parallax. Distance = 1000 / parallax puts each star at x, y, z in parsecs around the Sun. For the simulation we take the N stars closest to the median position of the whole sample, so every smaller subset sits inside the larger ones.

The simulation

Every star pulls on every other star

Each step computes all N² pair forces with Plummer softening. Stars that come closer than the merge radius become one star, keeping mass and momentum. Then every star gets a kick and drifts. All stars start at rest, so the ball first falls in on itself; close encounters then throw some stars far out.

≈ 10⁶
pair forces per step at N = 1,000. Doubling N quadruples the work.
9,800 yr
per step: Δt = 0.01 time units of 0.978 Myr each
0.01 pc
softening ε and merge radius, about 2,000 AU
v = 0
at the start. Proper motions and radial velocities are not used yet.

Runtime

Almost all the time goes into one function

99.5%

of the runtime is spent in compute_accelerations, a 40-line function. Measured in results.csv: gaia_nearest_1000, 2,000 steps, 168.9 of 169.6 s. With 5,000 stars it is 99.6%.

Share of codeSerialImplementation.py, 919 lines
compute_accelerations: 40 of 919 lines (4%) · click to jump to a section
Share of runtime169.6 s, one process
Forces 168.9 s (99.5%) · plotting 0.65 s (0.4%) · everything else 0.11 s (0.07%)

So there is one place where MPI pays off. Everything outside the force computation is currently so small that it barely slows the run down, even if it stays serial. That changes once Numba makes the kernel faster: then communication and the serial remainder start to count.

Each row is a target star i, each column a source star j. The matrix is cut into blocks, and each tile is one piece of work. The three schemes from the assignment compute exactly the same tiles; they only distribute them differently and exchange different data. Click a tile to pick a rank.

Pitfalls

      
Where the rewrite gets tricky

    

    

      

        
Merging
MPI-SYNC

        
N changes, the blocks have to be redistributed, and chains of close stars cross rank boundaries. Use --merge-radius 0 for the scaling runs. Otherwise treat merging as a rare event: gather everything, merge identically on every rank, redistribute.

      

      

        
Shared stop
MPI-SYNC

        
Today every process checks the time limit and Ctrl+C/SIGTERM on its own. If one rank stops a step early, the others wait forever in the next Allgatherv. Fix: one comm.allreduce(stop, op=MPI.LOR) per step.

      

      

        
Uneven blocks
MPI-KOMM

        
If N is not divisible by P, you need Allgatherv and Gatherv with counts and displs. The ring needs equal-sized buffers: pad every block to the largest one and give the padding stars mass 0.

      

      

        
Output
MPI-RANK0

        
print, results.csv, --save-final and plots on rank 0 only, after the data has arrived there via Gatherv or reduce. Cluster nodes have no display: matplotlib.use("Agg").

      

      

        
Kernel first
MPI-PARALLEL

        
The Python loop manages about 2·10⁷ pairs per second. Each rank then computes for so long that communication hardly registers and the scaling looks better than it is. Numba first, then measure.

      

    

  


  

    

      
Cluster runs · 10 Nov 2026

      
Eight ranks, 7.8 times faster

      
First runs of the MPI version on the DTU cluster: block decomposition with Allgatherv, all ranks on one node (Intel Xeon E5-2650 v4, 24 cores). Serial and MPI each ran 100 steps on the same node with the same 5,000 stars. No stars merged.

    

    

      
7.76×

      
faster with 8 ranks on gaia_nearest_5000: 2,499 ms per step serial, 322 ms with MPI. That is 97% of the ideal 8×. A repeat on a second node gives 7.77×.

The 3% missing from 8× come from waiting for the slowest rank and from a little more force time per rank than an eighth of the serial run, likely because eight processes share the caches and memory bandwidth of one node. Sending the positions costs next to nothing: 0.15 ms per step against 322 ms of compute.

  


  

    

      
Cluster runs · 8 ranks

      
Compute grows with N², communication with N

      
Three problem sizes with 8 ranks each, all with merge radius 0.001 pc on nodes of the same type. Twice the stars make a step 3.8 times slower, three times the stars 8.4 times. The data the ranks exchange grows only 2× and 3×. So the larger the problem, the smaller the share of communication: 0.04% of the run at 5,000 stars, 0.01% at 15,000.

One node only

        
All 8 ranks shared one node, so Allgatherv went through shared memory at 5.7–8.8 GB/s, not over the network. Runs spread over several nodes will show more communication.

      

      

        
Slow kernel

        
The Python kernel manages about 1·10⁷ pairs per second on one core of this node. That much compute hides the communication. With a faster kernel (Numba) the communication share will grow, as warned under “Kernel first”.

      

      

        
Short runs

        
100 steps, one run per configuration, no merges. A full strong-scaling series over 1 to 24 ranks and runs across nodes are still missing.
